The Day I Went for an Upanyasam and Came Back Spiritually Excavated

# The Day I Went for an Upanyasam and Came Back Spiritually Excavated

### One evening of upanyasam, three traffic diversions, four front-row maamas, one power cut, and a final spiritual lesson delivered by the sabha canteen.

[](https://substack.com/@amaruvi)

If you have not visited Mylapore recently, let me update you.

Mylapore is no longer a neighbourhood in Chennai.

It is a live infrastructure lab.

It is a collaborative excavation exercise.

It is a government-backed open-world video game called **Find the Sabha Without Damaging Your Suspension**.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

There was a time when Mylapore meant very simple things.

Kapaleeswarar temple.  
December season.  
Filter coffee.  
Sabha canteen idli.  
Mamis in Kanchipuram silk.  
Maamas who could identify your grandfather, your *gothram*, your school, your native place, and your likely salary bracket simply by looking at your forehead and the quality of your slippers.

Now Mylapore means only one thing.

**Diversion.**

Not spiritual diversion.  
Traffic diversion.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Metro Rail digs one road.

Metro Water digs the next.

The Telephone Department digs a third road to repair the cable damaged while repairing the pipe damaged during Metro work.

The Corporation then arrives, surveys the situation, and concludes that one more road must be dug in the public interest, purely to maintain narrative continuity.

Government departments may not speak to each other.

Their excavators certainly do.

Somewhere there is clearly a WhatsApp group called **Mylapore Digging Coordination Committee**.

One man is posting:  
“Mapla, Luz side work over. You take Kutchery Road tomorrow. Leave one majestic trench near the sabha entrance. Senior citizens also need adventure in life.”

Another is replying:  
“Done sir. Also cutting one water line for realism.”

A third asks:  
“Parking fully blocked or partially blocked?”

And some visionary bureaucrat types:  
“Fully. Let them grow spiritually. Cut the Air Tel line as Deepavali bonus.”

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Every Mylapore Outing Is Now a Pilgrimage

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Last weekend I had a modest plan.

Attend one upanyasam.  
Eat tiffin in the canteen.  
Come back home alive.

That is all.

In old Mylapore, this would have been called “going out in the evening.”

In present-day Mylapore, it requires route planning, tyre confidence, blood pressure control, and a willingness to forgive the State Government in advance.

The moment you leave home, Google Maps itself becomes philosophical.

It begins bravely.

“Head north.”

Two barricades later, it becomes uncertain.

“Take the next left.”

There is no next left. There is only one traffic policeman, three autos, four bikes, one cow, and a pile of sand large enough to start a sans storm.

Then the voice changes.

“Recalculating.”

After the fourth diversion, it sounds irritated.

“Recalculating.”

After the sixth, it sounds like a relative who opposed your marriage.

“Are you sure you need this upanyasam? Can’t you sit at home, open YouTube, and hear the same Bhagavatam in peace?”

This is where Google Maps fundamentally misunderstands the Mylapore mind.

You can hear Bhagavatam anywhere.

But can YouTube give you sabha canteen pongal?

Can YouTube give you one steel tumbler of dangerously good coffee served by a man who looks at you as if you personally ruined his token system?

Can YouTube give you front-row maamas conducting peer review of the speaker before he has even arrived?

No.

For that, one must suffer.

## Parking in Mylapore Is a Vedantic Test

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

By the time I reached the sabha, I had already crossed enough mud, barricades, one-ways, no-entry boards, and mysteriously parked share autos to qualify for hardship allowance.

Parking outside the hall looked like a family property dispute.

Cars were standing at angles unknown to geometry.

Scooters were leaning against each other for emotional support.

One Activa from 2004 had occupied a legal spot with the calm confidence of an old Mylapore resident who had clearly parked there during the Vajpayee government and simply never left.

I found one narrow gap between a Swift, a scooter, and what appeared to be an abandoned mixer-grinder carton, whispered “Kapali kaapathu,” and pushed my vehicle into it.

If the Mahabharata had included parallel parking near Luz, the war would have ended in one day. Nobody would have had the emotional energy for eighteen.

## The Real Programme Is Always in the Audience

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The speaker may be on stage.

But the true event in any Mylapore sabha is the audience.

Particularly the front-row maamas.

These men are not attendees. They are institutions. Governments may change. Children may move to Dallas. Mylapore houses may become apartment blocks with names like *Sri Vari Enclave*. But front-row maama opinion remains untouched by time, inflation, and urban decay.

Before the speaker had even entered, the review meeting had already begun.

One maama leaned over and said, “Last week he rushed the second slokam.”

Another nodded. “Correct. Also the Sanskrit pronunciation is not as weighty as before.”

A third said, “Pre-pandemic he was much better. Now he has become topical.”

That phrase — *he has become topical* — in Mylapore is equivalent to saying a Carnatic vocalist has started using karaoke support. It is not praise.

In any other city, people attend a discourse and then discuss it.

In Mylapore, the review is ready by 6:10 pm. The discourse begins at 6:30.

The maamas do not need to hear the full lecture. They can sense quality the way migratory birds sense weather.

One of them had the unmistakable face of a man who had attended 117 discourses this year and approved of exactly four.

Not good.  
Approved.

That is the highest honour available in this ecosystem.

## The Mami Intelligence Bureau Is More Efficient Than RAW

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Across the aisle, the mamis were conducting their own summit.

One lady walked in wearing a new Kanchipuram saree.

That was enough.

Within seven seconds, a complete intelligence assessment had been completed.

Which shop in T Nagar.  
Whether bought during Aadi sale.  
Whether the daughter in New Jersey had sponsored it.  
Approximate price bracket.  
Whether the zari was original or “these days all are saying pure, but who knows.”

Not one word was spoken in the first minute.

Everything was conveyed through the ancient Mylapore signalling system: one slight eyebrow lift, one measured look at the pallu, one brief tightening of the lips that can mean anything from admiration to a thirty-year grudge over a Navaratri *vethalai paaku* slight.

No intelligence agency on earth can compete with a sabha mami wearing bifocals and carrying unresolved social data from 1989.

A Mylapore mami does not merely see a saree.

She sees the family economy, the daughter’s H1B status, the son-in-law’s bonus cycle, and the exact degree of audacity involved in wearing such a border to a Saturday discourse.

## Enter the NRI Pilgrim

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Then came the NRI.

Usually from New Jersey.  
Sometimes California.  
Occasionally Singapore.  
But spiritually always New Jersey.

He arrived in a brand-new veshti with the stiffness of an unopened wedding return gift. Every few minutes he adjusted it with the concentration of a bomb disposal expert.

He carried an iPhone with too many cameras, a premium steel tumbler, and the expression of a man who had returned to “reconnect with his roots,” provided the roots came with air-conditioning and reliable mobile signal.

He took photos of everything.

Temple gopuram.  
Barricade.  
Kutcheri poster.  
One sleeping maama.  
The canteen token board.  
His own coffee.  
One cow standing near a trench looking more settled than most humans.

By now his Instagram story would have gone live:

**“Back in Mylapore after 14 years. Feeling grounded. Feeling rooted. So much heritage. So much stillness. \#Tradition \#MylaporeDiaries \#SacredSpaces \#FilterCoffeeSoul”**

Stillness, incidentally, was not visible anywhere within a three-kilometre radius.

> At one point he asked a volunteer, with genuine spiritual hunger,
> “Where can I experience the real old Mylapore?”
>
> The volunteer, who had clearly survived fifteen December Seasons and
> at least two Metro phases, didn’t even blink.
>
> “Go outside, take left after the third barricade. If you fall into one
> trench and still come out with coffee in hand, that is real Mylapore.”

## Advaita Inside. JCB Outside.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The upanyasam finally began.

Good opening slokam. Calm voice. Nice modulation. Promising start.

For two full minutes, there was peace.

Then the jackhammer outside began.

**THUD. THUD. THUD.**

The speaker said, “Everything in this world is temporary…”

**BRRRRRRRRR.**

A JCB reversed outside.

**BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. GRRR.. GRRR… BEEP.**

There was something so perfect about this that I almost wanted to applaud the Aadi-Talam in the JCB signal.

Inside the hall: Advaita, detachment, the fleeting nature of material life.

Outside the hall: Metro work, demonstrating the fleeting nature of the road itself.

The speaker spoke of transcending worldly attachment.

Outside, a man in a fluorescent vest was literally removing the world.

If Adi Shankara had lived in present-day Mylapore, half his commentaries would have included route diversions and a paragraph on temporary barricades as metaphor.

## The Sabha Canteen Is the Real Seat of Power

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Let us not overstate the role of spirituality here.

The sabha canteen is the true parliament of Mylapore.

Every hall has at least five men who appear to be listening to the discourse but are in fact conducting live surveillance of the canteen entrance.

They know exactly when the first batch of idli comes out.

They know whether the vadai is crisp that day.

They know if coffee is in steel tumbler or paper cup, and if it is paper cup, they will hold that against the management until Vaikunta Ekadasi.

That evening, midway through the discourse, a whisper moved across the back rows with the urgency of war intelligence.

“Idli vandhachu.”

That was all.

No slogan in modern Tamil politics has ever mobilised a demographic this efficiently.

Men who had spent the previous twenty minutes nodding gravely at the concept of detachment suddenly became logistics experts.

“Soft-aa?”

“Very soft.”

“Chutney?”

“Excellent.”

“Podi?”

“Yes.”

“Ghee?”

“Plenty.”

This is not food discussion. This is tactical planning.

If ISRO recruited from sabha canteen regulars, Chandrayaan would have landed directly in front of the token counter and ordered Pongal.

## One Political Reference and the Sabha Wakes Up

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The discourse was going well. The speaker moved elegantly between scripture and modern life.

> From Vyasa to WhatsApp, Valmiki to Vibe Coding.   
> From maya to mobile addiction. From Futile Existence to Full Stack
> development.  
> From ancient kings to family groups in which one retired uncle keeps
> sending anti-China videos and miracle-cure forwards at 5:12 every
> morning.

The audience was pleased. This is exactly the right amount of modernity for Mylapore: enough to feel relevant, not enough to threaten inheritance patterns.

Then the speaker made one passing contemporary political reference.

Nothing major. Just a comparison. One casual mention of a charismatic southern public figure attracting youth support. The one that formed government with Instagram reels.

You would have thought someone had smuggled garlic into the temple kitchen.

The hall woke up.

The under-40 crowd became alert.

One maama removed his glasses and cleaned them with aggressive disappointment.

A mami paused and let out a mild-cough.

The trustees looked like men mentally recalculating donor risk.

The speaker realised at once that he had touched live wire.

He returned to the Mahabharata with the speed of a man backing away from an electric fence.

## Then Came the Power Cut

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Coffee was consumed. Idlis vanished. Intermission reviews were exchanged.

One maama declared that the speaker had “started well but must reduce his tendency to become current-affairs-oriented.”

The second half began.

Exactly when the speaker reached an important point, the microphone died.

Not faded. But Died.

Immediately retired engineers in the audience rose from their seats with the sense of purpose usually seen only in emergency wards and temple kitchens.

One blamed the amplifier.

One blamed earthing.

One blamed voltage fluctuation.

One blamed Metro digging outside.

One blamed the general decline of manufacturing standards after liberalisation.

Before any consensus could be reached, TANGEDCO entered the conversation.

Power cut.

Total darkness. Nothing to do with the previous regime squirrel or the current ones.

At once forty mobile flashlights came on.

The hall looked like a Coldplay concert organised by Mylapore Fine Arts and sponsored by the Electricity Board.

And then the deepest instinct of civilisation took over.

**Everybody started looking for their slippers.**

Nothing strips away education, income, ideology and social standing faster than a power cut in a sabha.

Degrees vanish.  
Vedanta vanishes.  
NRI accent vanishes.  
Only chappal remains.

One maama emerged triumphantly holding someone else’s Woodland sandal like Arjuna recovering Gandiva.

Another found only his left slipper and stared at it with the expression of a man reviewing all his karmas from previous births.

One formidable mami quietly occupied a strategic position near the footwear rack and refused to move until her Bata pair was produced.

Someone shouted, “Whose Paragon, size 8?”

Four people turned.

For three minutes there was no caste, no class, no sect, no political leaning, no Carnatic preference.

Only slipper recovery.

If the Planning Commission had ever studied India at its most authentic, it should have spent one evening outside a Mylapore sabha during a power cut.

## The Final Punchline

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Eventually power supply resumed.

The microphone came back to life.

People found most of their footwear, though not always in original pairs.

The speaker adjusted the mike, looked at this audience of spiritually elevated but physically exhausted devotees, and delivered his concluding line:

**“Therefore, as we have all seen today, everything material in life is temporary.”**

The hall burst into laughter.

Because what else can you do?

Outside, the barricades were still there.

The trenches were still there.

Traffic was still not moving.

The jackhammer had resumed its tani avartanam.

And Mylapore remained gloriously itself.

A place where upanyasam and excavation coexist.

A place where mamis can conduct forensic saree analysis in under ten seconds.

A place where the canteen has more operational clarity than civic administration.

A place where NRIs come searching for “roots” and go back with podi, coffee powder, one brass *vilakku*, three packets of *manathakkali vathal*, and mild lower-back pain from wearing veshti incorrectly.

As I crossed one more mud trench and made my way home, I realised something.

Maybe Mylapore itself is the upanyasam.

The traffic teaches patience.  
The parking teaches surrender.  
The power cut teaches detachment.  
The canteen teaches gratitude.  
The lost slipper teaches non-possession.

And the orange barricades teach the final truth.

**Even if you complete all your karma, attain moksha, and escape the cycle of rebirth, the road near Luz Corner will still be under repair.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**If you have ever lost a slipper at a sabha, parked near Luz with only divine support, or returned from America convinced Mylapore still looked exactly like 1987, write in. And if you know someone in New Jersey, Sunnyvale, Sydney, Singapore, West Mambalam or West Mylapore who will forward this with the subject line “So true da,” send it to them immediately. Kapaleeswara will ensure you get married soon and if you are already married, Kapali will help you get even with the samsaram.**
